synonyms: ["Chronic Pancreatis", "Long-lasting Inflammation Of The Pancreas", "Long-term Inflammation Of The Pancreas", "Persistent Pancreatitis"]
conventional_description: Chronic pancreatitis is a persistent inflammation of the pancreas that leads to irreversible damage, fibrosis, and loss of both exocrine and endocrine function. The main symptom is recurrent or constant upper abdominal pain, often radiating to the back, worsened by eating. As the disease progresses, patients may develop malabsorption, steatorrhea (fatty stools), weight loss, and diabetes due to destruction of insulin-producing cells. Diagnosis typically involves imaging such as CT, MRI, or endoscopic ultrasound, along with tests of pancreatic function.
conventional_treatments: Standard management includes pain control with analgesics, pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy to aid digestion, and insulin for diabetes when it develops. Patients are advised to abstain from alcohol, follow a low-fat diet, and eat small frequent meals. In some cases, endoscopic procedures or surgery are used to drain pseudocysts or relieve ductal obstructions. Antioxidant supplements are sometimes recommended to reduce oxidative stress.
tcm_understanding:
TCM understands chronic pancreatitis primarily through the lens of the Spleen and Stomach, the organs responsible for transforming food into Qi and blood. When the Spleen's Qi is weak - from poor diet, overwork, or constitutional deficiency - digestion becomes sluggish.
Food is not properly transformed, leading to bloating, loose stools, fatigue, and a dull, nagging upper abdominal pain. This Spleen Qi Deficiency is often the root soil in which chronic inflammation takes hold.
The Liver also plays a crucial role. Emotional stress, frustration, and anger cause Liver Qi to stagnate. Instead of flowing smoothly, this stuck Qi can surge sideways and attack the Stomach, disrupting its downward rhythm. The result is a distending pain that radiates to the ribs, frequent belching, and symptoms that flare with emotional upset.
Over time, if the Liver's stagnation combines with dietary excess - alcohol, greasy foods - it generates Damp-Heat, a toxic mix that clogs the pancreas and leads to bitter taste, nausea, and even jaundice.
As the condition lingers, the persistent inflammation and repeated injury create deeper stagnation. Qi and Blood become stuck, causing fixed, stabbing pain that is tender to touch.
In some patients, the Spleen's warming Yang becomes depleted, leading to cold hands and feet, a need for hot water bottles, and loose stools with undigested food.
This is why one Western diagnosis can present so differently: the dull ache of deficiency, the distending stress pain, and the sharp fixed pain are each a different TCM pattern requiring a different treatment.

tcm_diagnosis:
A TCM practitioner begins by asking you to describe the pain in your own words - is it dull and nagging, or sharp and stabbing? They will also ask what makes it better or worse, and whether it comes with bloating, nausea, or changes in bowel habits. The answers are the first clues that separate deficiency patterns from acute flare-ups.
If the pain is a persistent dull ache with bloating, fatigue, poor appetite, and loose stools, the root is likely Spleen and Stomach Qi Deficiency. The tongue is pale and puffy, often with teeth marks, and the pulse feels weak and thready. This is the most common underlying pattern in chronic pancreatitis.
When emotional stress brings on a distending pain that radiates to the ribs, along with belching and nausea, the picture shifts to Liver Qi Stagnation invading the Stomach. The tongue may look slightly dusky, and the pulse becomes wiry. The pain tends to move around and is closely tied to mood.
A sudden episode of epigastric fullness, bitter taste in the mouth, nausea, and possibly yellowing of the skin or eyes points to Liver and Gallbladder Damp-Heat. The tongue coating is thick, greasy, and yellow, and the pulse is rapid and slippery or wiry. This pattern often flares after drinking alcohol or eating rich, fatty foods.
If symptoms appear shortly after a heavy meal - marked abdominal distension, sour or foul belching, and a thick greasy tongue coating - the practitioner suspects Food Stagnation in the Stomach. The pulse is usually slippery. This pattern is acute and directly tied to dietary indiscretion.
When the illness has persisted for years, the pain may become fixed and stabbing, with tenderness that refuses pressure. The tongue turns purplish with dark spots, and the pulse is wiry and choppy. This indicates Qi and Blood Stagnation, a deeper level of chronic damage.
If the dull ache improves with warmth and pressure, and you feel cold in the hands and feet, the deficiency has deepened into Spleen Yang Deficiency. The tongue is pale, swollen, and wet, and the pulse is deep, slow, and weak. This pattern adds a clear cold component to the digestive weakness.

patterns.symptoms: ["Dull, lingering epigastric pain", "Bloating and fullness after eating", "Poor appetite with loose stools", "Deep fatigue and weak limbs", "Sallow or pale complexion"]
patterns.worse_with: Overeating or large meals, Cold foods and drinks, Overwork and exhaustion, Irregular meal times, Emotional stress, anger or worry
patterns.better_with: Light, bland meals, Warm, easily digested congee, Rest after eating, Gentle walking, Warm compress on the abdomen
patterns.why_this_happens: In TCM, the Spleen transforms food into Qi and blood. When its Qi is weak, digestion falters, leading to bloating, poor appetite, loose stools, and deep fatigue. Over time, this deficiency creates a chronic state of inflammation in the pancreas because the organ system responsible for digestion cannot keep up, producing persistent dull pain and malabsorption.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, puffy, with tooth marks and a thin white coating. Pulse: weak, soft, especially deficient at the right Guan (Spleen) position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Spleen Qi deficiency means the digestive fire is weak. Overeating, cold raw foods, and irregular meals overwhelm the Spleen, worsening bloating and fatigue. Rest and warmth conserve Qi, while small, warm, easily digestible meals give the Spleen a manageable load, allowing it to recover.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat small, frequent meals of warm, cooked foods like congee, steamed vegetables, and well-cooked grains. Avoid raw, cold, greasy, or heavy foods that tax digestion. Gentle exercise like walking or Tai Chi helps move Qi, but do not overexert. Rest after meals and avoid eating when stressed.

patterns.symptoms: ["Distending, bloating pain in the upper abdomen", "Pain radiates to the rib area on one or both sides", "Symptoms clearly worsen with emotional stress or frustration", "Frequent belching, acid reflux or sour regurgitation", "Irritability, moodiness and frequent sighing"]
patterns.worse_with: Emotional stress, anger or worry, Greasy, fried or spicy foods, Alcohol consumption, Eating late at night, Prolonged sitting and inactivity
patterns.better_with: Reducing emotional stress, Warm compress on the abdomen, Light, bland meals, Gentle walking, Deep breathing and sighing it out
patterns.why_this_happens: Emotional stress, frustration and anger cause the Liver Qi to stagnate. Instead of flowing smoothly, this stuck Qi surges sideways and attacks the Stomach, disrupting its natural downward rhythm. The result is distending pain in the upper abdomen that often spreads to the rib cage, along with belching, acid reflux and nausea - classic signs of a Liver-Stomach disharmony that frequently triggers or worsens chronic pancreatitis flare-ups.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: normal or slightly red body with redder sides, thin white coat. Pulse: wiry (弦 xián), like a taut guitar string.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Emotional stress is the main driver of this pattern - it makes Liver Qi surge and invade the Stomach, so anything that calms the mind and smooths the Qi brings relief. Greasy, spicy food and alcohol create Damp-Heat and burden the Stomach, adding fuel to the fire. Gentle movement and warmth help unblock stuck Qi, while small bland meals give the digestive system a chance to recover without overwhelming it.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid alcohol and cut back on greasy, fried or spicy foods, as they fuel stagnation and heat. Eat smaller, regular meals and chew well - this gives your Stomach less work to do. Build daily stress-management habits like walking, deep breathing or gentle yoga to keep Liver Qi moving smoothly.

patterns.why_this_happens: When alcohol, fatty foods, or emotional stress overload the Liver and Gallbladder, Dampness and Heat build up inside. This toxic mix can spill over into the pancreas, clogging its channels and blocking the normal flow of Qi and Blood. The result is the inflamed, swollen sensation and the bitter taste, jaundice, and digestive upset typical of an acute flare.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body, red sides, thick yellow greasy coating. Pulse: wiry, slippery, and rapid.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Alcohol, greasy, and spicy foods directly introduce Dampness and Heat, the two pathological factors at the core of this pattern. Emotional frustration stagnates Liver Qi, which then turns into Heat and combines with Dampness. Cooling, bland foods and bitter herbs help the body drain Dampness and clear Heat, while rest and stress management allow Liver Qi to flow smoothly again, preventing the buildup that inflames the pancreas.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eliminate alcohol, fried, greasy, and spicy foods completely during a flare. Base meals around lightly cooked vegetables, mung beans, barley, and small amounts of lean protein. Bitter greens like dandelion help drain Damp-Heat. Eat smaller, more frequent meals to avoid overloading the pancreas.

patterns.symptoms: ["Upper abdominal bloating and distending pain", "Sour, rotten-smelling belching", "Pain and bloating relieved after vomiting", "Thick greasy or curd-like tongue coating", "Aversion to food and its smell"]
patterns.worse_with: Overeating or eating too quickly, Greasy, fried or spicy foods, Alcohol consumption, Eating late at night
patterns.better_with: Vomiting undigested food, Skipping a meal or fasting, Warm, easily digested congee, Gentle walking
patterns.why_this_happens: When you eat more than your stomach can handle, or consume rich, greasy foods too quickly, digestion backs up. Undigested food sits and ferments, producing turbid Qi that rises as foul belching and acid reflux. The stomach becomes painfully bloated because food is not moving downward as it should, directly triggering the upper abdominal distension and discomfort of chronic pancreatitis.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: body may be normal, but the coating is thick, greasy, even curd-like, thickest in the centre. Pulse: slippery (滑 Huá), full and prominent at the right middle (Stomach) position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Overeating overwhelms the stomach's ability to 'rotten and ripen' food, creating a physical blockage of turbid, fermenting mass that obstructs Qi flow. Vomiting mechanically empties this accumulation, which is why pain and bloating instantly improve. Greasy, rich foods and alcohol are the hardest to digest and directly feed this stagnation, while a light diet and gentle movement help Stomach Qi descend, preventing food from sitting and spoiling.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat smaller, lighter meals and chew thoroughly. Avoid raw, cold, and greasy foods that burden the stomach. A short walk after eating helps Qi descend. If you feel uncomfortably full, skip the next meal or have just a light congee to give your digestion a rest.

patterns.worse_with: Emotional stress, anger or worry, Greasy, heavy meals, Alcohol consumption, Pressure on the abdomen, Overwork and exhaustion
patterns.better_with: Gentle walking, Warm compress on the abdomen, Light, bland meals, Rest and lying down, Avoiding alcohol and rich foods
patterns.why_this_happens: When chronic pancreatitis drags on, the persistent inflammation and repeated injury create local stagnation. Qi, which should flow smoothly, becomes stuck, and over time the blood vessels in the pancreas and surrounding tissues become congested and knotted. This is what produces the characteristic fixed, stabbing pain that is tender to the touch.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: purple or dark body with scattered stasis spots, distended sublingual veins, thin white coat. Pulse: wiry (弦 xián) and choppy (涩 sè), like a taut string scraping bamboo.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Emotional stress knots the Liver Qi, which is the driving force behind smooth circulation; when Qi stagnates, Blood congeals, making the stabbing pain worse. Heavy, greasy food and alcohol brew dampness and heat, creating a sticky obstruction that further blocks Qi and Blood flow. Gentle movement and warmth, on the other hand, coax the Qi to flow and the Blood to circulate, gradually melting the stagnation. Small meals and rest give the digestive system a break, so the body can focus on clearing the long-standing stasis.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat small, frequent, easily digestible meals-think soups, congees, and steamed vegetables-to avoid overloading the digestive system. Avoid alcohol completely and steer clear of greasy, fried, or spicy foods that create dampness and heat, which further obstruct Qi. Gentle daily movement like walking or tai chi helps keep Qi and Blood moving, but avoid heavy exercise that strains the abdomen. Managing emotional stress is crucial, as frustration and anger directly worsen Liver stagnation.

patterns.worse_with: Cold foods and drinks, Cold, damp weather, Overwork and exhaustion, Emotional stress, anger or worry
patterns.better_with: Warm compress on the abdomen, Eating warm, cooked foods, Rest and lying down
patterns.why_this_happens: In TCM, the Spleen's Yang is the digestive fire that transforms food into energy and keeps the body warm. When this fire dwindles, the middle burner becomes cold and sluggish, failing to digest food properly. This leads to a buildup of Dampness and Cold in the pancreas region, causing the dull, persistent pain and bloating of chronic pancreatitis. The body's overall energy plummets, and cold signs appear because Yang can no longer warm the limbs or drive metabolism.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, puffy, tender body with scalloped edges, white slippery coating. Pulse: deep, slow, and weak, especially at the right guan (Spleen/Stomach) position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Spleen Yang is the body's digestive fire. Cold foods and weather directly extinguish this fire, worsening pain and bloating. Warmth, both from external heat and warm cooked foods, rekindles Yang and restores digestive function. Rest conserves Qi that would otherwise be spent on activity, allowing the Spleen to recover its transformative power.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked foods like soups, stews, and congees. Strictly avoid cold, raw, and greasy foods that further chill the Spleen. Keep your abdomen warm with a hot water bottle or warm compress. Gentle daily movement like walking helps Qi flow without depleting your energy.

faqs.question: Can TCM cure chronic pancreatitis?
faqs.answer: TCM cannot reverse the structural damage or fibrosis already present, but it can significantly reduce the frequency and severity of flare-ups, manage pain, and improve digestion and quality of life. By strengthening the Spleen, clearing Damp-Heat, and moving stagnant Qi and Blood, TCM addresses the underlying imbalances that drive the disease, often slowing its progression.

faqs.question: How does acupuncture help with pancreatic pain?
faqs.answer: Acupuncture stimulates specific points that regulate the flow of Qi through the digestive organs, reduce inflammation, and trigger the release of the body's natural painkillers. Key points like Zusanli (ST-36) and Zhongwan (REN-12) help calm the Stomach and strengthen the Spleen, while Taichong (LR-3) moves Liver Qi to relieve stress-related pain. Many patients experience pain relief during or shortly after a session.

faqs.question: What foods should I avoid if I have chronic pancreatitis?
faqs.answer: You should strictly avoid alcohol, as it is a major trigger that creates Damp-Heat and damages the Liver and Spleen. Also avoid greasy, fried, or spicy foods, dairy products, and raw or cold foods, which all burden the digestive system. Instead, focus on warm, cooked, easily digestible meals like congee, steamed vegetables, and lean proteins. Eating small, frequent meals and chewing thoroughly is essential.

faqs.question: Can I take pancreatic enzymes with Chinese herbs?
faqs.answer: Yes, it is generally safe to combine them. To avoid any interference with digestion or absorption, take your herbal formula and pancreatic enzymes at different times of day - for example, herbs between meals and enzymes with meals. Always inform both your TCM practitioner and your medical doctor about all supplements and medications you are using.

faqs.question: How long until I feel better?
faqs.answer: Many people notice less bloating, nausea, and pain after meals within the first 2-4 weeks of treatment. However, full and lasting improvement depends on the pattern: excess conditions like Damp-Heat may clear quickly, while deep deficiency patterns require 3-6 months of consistent herbs, acupuncture, and dietary changes to rebuild the Spleen's strength and reduce pain significantly.

faqs.question: Do I need to stop drinking alcohol completely?
faqs.answer: Yes. From a TCM perspective, alcohol is a potent source of Damp-Heat that directly inflames the Liver and pancreas and undermines the Spleen's digestive function. Even small amounts can trigger flare-ups and prevent healing. Complete abstinence is one of the most important steps you can take for long-term relief.

research.title: Chronic Pancreatitis Integrated Chinese and Western Medicine Diagnosis and Treatment Consensus (2020)
research.description: This expert consensus, developed by the Chinese Association of Integrative Medicine, provides standardized TCM pattern differentiation and treatment protocols for chronic pancreatitis. It outlines six common patterns - including Spleen and Stomach Qi Deficiency, Liver Qi Stagnation invading the Stomach, and Liver and Gallbladder Damp-Heat - with corresponding herbal formulas and acupuncture points. The document serves as a key reference for integrating TCM into the management of chronic pancreatitis.

research.title: Traditional Chinese Medicine Diagnosis and Treatment Guideline for Chronic Pancreatitis (Grassroots Doctor Version)
research.description: Aimed at primary care practitioners, this guideline details the etiology, pathogenesis, and pattern identification of chronic pancreatitis in TCM. It emphasizes the root of Spleen and Stomach deficiency and the branches of Damp-Heat, Qi stagnation, and blood stasis. The guideline recommends specific herbal formulas like Si Jun Zi Tang, Chai Hu Shu Gan San, and Long Dan Xie Gan Tang, along with acupuncture protocols, based on pattern presentation.
